2027-04-21.title: Wednesday of the Fourth Week of Easter · St Anselm
readings: Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul
O God, let all the nations praise you! (or: Alleluia)
I have come as light into the world
2027-04-21.alt: Optional memorial: St Anselm, bishop and doctor of the Church (1033–1109). The Easter weekday readings are kept. Regina Caeli at noon until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-21.verse: I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me should not remain in the darkness.
theo: “The word of God continued to advance and gain adherents.” With this short line Luke closes the story of King Herod Agrippa, who had killed James and imprisoned Peter, and who then died miserably. Kings rise and fall; the word goes on. Then the scene moves to Antioch, where the Church has grown rich in gifts. Luke names five “prophets and teachers”: Barnabas from Cyprus, Simeon called Niger, which means “the black,” Lucius of Cyrene in North Africa, Manaen who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul of Tarsus. An African, a Cypriot, a man of the royal court, a former persecutor: already the Church is a gathering of nations and classes. And it is while they are at prayer that the Spirit speaks: “While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, ‘Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.’”

The first great missionary journey is born in the liturgy. The word Luke uses for “worshiping” is the word from which we get “liturgy.” The Church did not choose missionaries by vote or by talent; it fasted, prayed, listened, and then obeyed. “Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off.” And Luke adds: “being sent out by the Holy Spirit.” The community lays on hands; the Spirit sends. The two go down to the port of Seleucia, sail to Cyprus, and begin to proclaim the word in the synagogues at Salamis, with young John Mark as their helper. The Psalm is the perfect prayer for this moment of mission: “Let the peoples praise you, O God; let all the peoples praise you.” The blessing given to Israel is meant to shine out to every nation, so that “your way may be known upon earth, your saving power among all nations.”

In the Gospel Jesus cries aloud, almost his last public words in John before the Last Supper: “Whoever believes in me believes not in me but in him who sent me. And whoever sees me sees him who sent me.” Jesus is not a messenger who points away from himself; to see him is to see the Father. “I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me should not remain in the darkness.” And he says that he did not come to condemn: “I came not to judge the world, but to save the world.” Yet the word he speaks is not empty. It will stand on the last day as the measure of our lives, because it is the Father's own word. Today the Church remembers St Anselm, the monk of Bec and Archbishop of Canterbury, who spent his life seeking to understand this light. His famous motto was “faith seeking understanding.” He did not believe because he had understood; he believed so that he might understand. He prayed: teach me to seek you, and show yourself to me when I seek. For Anselm, thinking about God was itself a way of praying, and prayer was the light in which thought could see.
conn: Grandson of Herod the Great, king of Judea AD 41–44. He executed James the brother of John and arrested Peter (Acts 12:1–4); his sudden death at Caesarea is told in Acts 12:20–23 and also by the Jewish historian Josephus.
Niger is Latin for “black.” He may have been an African; some have suggested he is Simon of Cyrene (Mark 15:21), but this cannot be shown.
A syntrophos of Herod Antipas: brought up with him as a boy, perhaps a foster brother. The Gospel reached even the circles of the court that had killed John the Baptist.
The Greek leitourgountōn, from which comes “liturgy.” The mission of Paul begins in public prayer and fasting.

An ancient sign of blessing and of handing on a task (Numbers 27:18–23). Here it commissions Barnabas and Saul for a particular mission; in the Church it is the sign used in Confirmation and Holy Orders.
Cousin of Barnabas (Colossians 4:10), whose mother's house in Jerusalem was a meeting place of the Church (Acts 12:12). Tradition identifies him with St Mark the Evangelist.
John holds together the present and the future: judgement happens already in the response to Christ (John 3:18), and it will be revealed fully on the last day.

Born at Aosta in the Alps (1033), monk, prior and abbot of Bec in Normandy, Archbishop of Canterbury from 1093. Twice exiled for defending the freedom of the Church. Author of the Proslogion and Cur Deus Homo (Why God Became Man). Declared Doctor of the Church in 1720. Died 21 April 1109.
altar: The mission of Barnabas and Saul was born while the Church was “worshiping the Lord and fasting.” Every mission of the Church comes from the altar and returns to it.

Christ came as light into the world. The paschal candle beside the altar this whole season is the sign of that light, and at the consecration the Light of the world comes among us under the veil of bread and wine.
outline: Ask: when I have a big decision, do I pray and fast before I act?
Point 1 · Set apart for the work
The Spirit speaks during the liturgy at Antioch.
Whoever sees Jesus sees the Father.
St Anselm, thinker and man of prayer.
A monk at a desk by candlelight, pen in hand, praying before he writes.
“I have come as light into the world.”
live: Before the next important choice in your family or work, set aside a day of prayer and a small fast, as the Church at Antioch did.
Pray today for a missionary you know by name, perhaps a priest or sister from your parish serving in North India or abroad, and send them a message.
Bring one hidden thing into the light this week: a confession, an apology, a truth you have been avoiding.
Take one question about your faith that troubles you, and read about it in the Catechism, beginning and ending with a prayer, as Anselm did.
fathers: I do not seek to understand so that I may believe; I believe so that I may understand. For this too I believe: that unless I believe, I shall not understand.

Come now, little man, leave your busy cares for a while and rest a little in God. Enter the inner room of your mind, shut out everything except God, and say: now, Lord my God, teach my heart where and how to seek you, where and how to find you.
Christ the light says: whoever believes in me will not remain in darkness. This shows that he found all in darkness; but he wills that they should not remain in it.
magis: “Faith seeks understanding”: the words of St Anselm. A believer desires to know better the One in whom he has put his faith.
Fides et Ratio 42 (St John Paul II, 1998)
St Anselm shows that faith and reason, far from being opposed, help each other: the intelligence of faith.
The laying on of hands, a sign of the Holy Spirit.
The Holy Spirit is the principal agent of mission, at work in the Church from Pentecost onward.
Prayer as a battle and the error of separating prayer from action and thought.
saints: Bishop and Doctor of the Church. A gentle and humble monk who became a fearless archbishop; a great thinker who wrote some of the most tender prayers of the Middle Ages, including prayers to the Blessed Virgin Mary, whom he called the mother of all things made new. Called the Father of Scholasticism.
23 Apr: St George; St Adalbert. 24 Apr: St Fidelis of Sigmaringen. 25 Apr: Fifth Sunday of Easter.
2027-04-21.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, light of the world, whoever sees you sees the Father who sent you. Shine into the darkness of our minds and hearts. As your Spirit set apart Barnabas and Saul while your Church was at prayer, call and send in our time missionaries, priests and religious, and make every one of us ready to go where you send. By the prayers of St Anselm, give us a faith that seeks to understand and an understanding that bows in love, so that we may know you more truly and love you more dearly. You live and reign for ever and ever. Alleluia. Amen.

quick: At Antioch, during worship and fasting, the Holy Spirit set apart Barnabas and Saul for mission.
Jesus: I have come as light into the world; whoever sees me sees him who sent me.
2027-04-21.action: Pray today for one missionary by name, and if you can, send them a word of support.
2027-04-21.question: Do I try to understand my faith better, or am I content to know only what I learned as a child?
catechism: The Holy Spirit, protagonist of mission.
kidsaint: Anselm grew up in the mountains of Italy and dreamed that God lived on the top of the highest peak. When he grew up he became a monk and spent his life thinking and praying about God. He became the Archbishop of Canterbury in England and was brave when the king tried to boss the Church. Lesson: we can use our minds to love God more, by learning about him and praying.
2027-04-21.special: Optional memorial of St Anselm: white vestments; the Easter weekday readings; Regina Caeli at noon.
term: In Latin fides quaerens intellectum, the phrase of St Anselm. Faith is not blind; the believer, already trusting God, uses the mind to understand more deeply what God has revealed. This is the task of theology (Catechism 158).

family.explain: In the church at Antioch the leaders were praying and fasting together. The Holy Spirit told them: choose Barnabas and Saul for a special work. So they prayed again, laid their hands on them, and sent them off to tell other countries about Jesus. That was the beginning of St Paul's great journeys.
family.intention: We pray for missionaries all over the world, especially those from our own parish and diocese.
family.ask: Ask: “What job might God be choosing each of us for?” Before the next family decision, decide to pray about it together first.

illus: A retired engineer in Thrissur, a daily communicant, kept a notebook of questions his grandson asked him about God: why does God allow suffering, how can bread become Jesus, how can three be one. He did not want to give lazy answers. So each evening, after the Rosary, he read a page of the Catechism and a page of the Fathers, and wrote down what he learned. After three years the notebook had become a small handwritten book. His grandson, now at a seminary, keeps it on his desk. On the first page the old man had written: I believe, so that I may understand.

pm.open: Holy Spirit, you set apart Barnabas and Saul during prayer. Speak to us now as we worship and listen. Alleluia. Amen.
share: While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:2). What is the Spirit asking of me?
Whoever sees me sees him who sent me (John 12:45). How has Jesus shown me the face of the Father?
I have come as light into the world (John 12:46). What darkness in my life needs his light?
pm.resp: O God, let all the nations praise you!
interc: For missionaries of our diocese and parish, that the Spirit may sustain them.
For those discerning a call to priesthood or religious life, that they may hear the Spirit's voice in prayer.
For theologians and teachers of the faith, that like St Anselm they may join study to prayer.
For those who live in darkness, that the light of Christ may reach them.
For our group, that we may pray and fast before every important decision.
pm.close: Father, through St Anselm you taught your Church to seek understanding in faith. Grant that we may believe more deeply, understand more clearly and love more ardently. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, in the church at Antioch the leaders are at prayer. They are worshiping and fasting. And in that prayer the Holy Spirit speaks: set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them (Acts 13:2). The greatest missionary journey in history began in a prayer meeting.

The Church did not choose Paul's mission by a committee vote. It prayed, it fasted, it listened, and it obeyed. Then they laid hands on them and sent them off. Whenever we have important decisions, in our families, our parishes, our lives, let us learn from Antioch: pray first, then act.

Look also at who those leaders were: a Cypriot, a man called Niger, the black, a man from Cyrene in Africa, a member of Herod's court, and a former persecutor. The Church was already one family of many nations.

In the Gospel Jesus cries out: I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me should not remain in the darkness (John 12:46). He did not come to condemn but to save. Whoever sees Jesus sees the Father.

Today we remember St Anselm, a monk who became Archbishop of Canterbury. He loved to think about God, but he always thought on his knees. He said: I believe, so that I may understand. He did not stop believing when he had questions; he took his questions into prayer.
Let us ask for that grace today: to let the light of Christ fill both our hearts and our minds, and to be ready, like Barnabas and Saul, to go where the Spirit sends us. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, when the leaders at Antioch were praying, the Holy Spirit chose Barnabas and Saul to go and tell the whole world about Jesus.
When we pray, God can tell us what he wants us to do too. Jesus is the light of the world. Let us say: Jesus, shine in my heart!

concl: The mission of the Church is born in worship and is the work of the Holy Spirit.
Christ is the light in which we see the Father, and like St Anselm we seek to understand what we believe.
